collections.title: Collections Framework Foundations
collections.summary: The Java Collections Framework is a standard set of interfaces, classes, and utility methods used to store and process groups of objects.
learningObjectives: Understand Collection, List, Set, Queue, Deque, and Map.
Choose a collection from order, duplicates, lookup, null, and concurrency needs.
Understand interface versus implementation.
Read Big-O complexity without memorizing it blindly.
explanation: In one line: The Java Collections Framework is a standard set of interfaces, classes, and utility methods used to store and process groups of objects.
An array can store many values, but its size is fixed. Collections add ready-made behavior such as growing, searching, removing, sorting, preventing duplicates, or finding a value by key.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: An array can store many values, but its size is fixed. Collections add ready-made behavior such as growing, searching, removing, sorting, preventing duplicates, or finding a value by key.
The framework separates what a structure promises from how it performs that promise. List, Set, Queue, and Map are contracts. ArrayList, HashSet, ArrayDeque, and HashMap are implementations.
Map belongs to the framework but does not extend Collection because it stores key-value pairs rather than individual elements.
detailSections.note: Think of the interfaces as requirements on a shopping list and implementations as different containers. You choose the container after you know whether order, uniqueness, fast lookup, or priority matters.

collections.title: List — ArrayList, LinkedList and CopyOnWriteArrayList
collections.summary: A List is an ordered sequence that keeps position, normally allows duplicates, and provides zero-based indexed access.
learningObjectives: Understand List properties and index rules.
Know the internal structure of ArrayList and LinkedList.
Choose ArrayList as the normal default.
Distinguish fixed-size, unmodifiable, view, and snapshot lists.
explanation: In one line: A List is an ordered sequence that keeps position, normally allows duplicates, and provides zero-based indexed access.
List is used when the sequence matters: first item, second item, and so on. Two equal values may appear at different positions.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: List is used when the sequence matters: first item, second item, and so on. Two equal values may appear at different positions.
Indexes start at 0. A list of size n has valid indexes 0 through n-1.

ArrayList is the normal choice because direct index reads are fast and its contiguous reference array is cache-friendly. LinkedList is useful only for specific deque/list workloads where you already have an iterator/node position.
detailSections.note: A List is like numbered seats in a row. Duplicate names are allowed, but each occurrence has its own seat number.

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: ArrayList stores element references in an internal array and keeps a separate size.
get(i) calculates the array position directly, so it is O(1).
add at the end stores the value if capacity exists; otherwise a larger array is allocated and references are copied.
Insert/remove near the front or middle shifts later array elements.
LinkedList stores each value in a node with previous and next links.
LinkedList get(i) walks nodes from the nearer end, so random index access is O(n).
CopyOnWriteArrayList writes create and publish a new array; existing iterators keep their old snapshot.
Exact ArrayList growth is an implementation detail, not a List API promise.
detailSections.note: Do not say LinkedList insertion is always O(1). Finding index i is O(n); only the link change is O(1) after the position is already known.

You need index access or frequent sequential traversal.
Most writes are append operations.
You want to sort a sequence without removing duplicate values.
detailSections.note: Avoid or rethink it when: membership lookup is the main operation (consider Set), you need key-value lookup (Map), or frequent front operations are required (ArrayDeque is usually clearer).

collections.title: Set — HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet
collections.summary: A Set stores unique elements; its equality rule and iteration order depend on the implementation.
learningObjectives: Understand uniqueness in hash-based and sorted sets.
Know the internal structures of HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet.
Choose a Set from order and performance needs.
Keep equality/hash/order fields stable while stored.
explanation: In one line: A Set stores unique elements; its equality rule and iteration order depend on the implementation.
Set answers the question: have I already seen this logical value? Adding an equal value does not create another member.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Set answers the question: have I already seen this logical value? Adding an equal value does not create another member.
HashSet defines duplicates through equals and hashCode. TreeSet defines duplicates through compareTo or Comparator: comparison result zero means the same sorted-set element.
LinkedHashSet keeps HashSet-style uniqueness and adds predictable insertion order.
detailSections.note: A Set is like an entry gate with a guest rule. HashSet checks an identity card using hash and equals; TreeSet places every guest in sorted order and considers comparison zero a duplicate.

table.title: Set — HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet at a glance
rows: Not stored; add returns false for an existing logical value.
HashSet/LinkedHashSet allow one null; natural-order TreeSet normally rejects null.
General-purpose Set implementations are not thread-safe.
Hash sets use equals/hashCode; sorted sets use comparison zero.
Dangerous when equality, hash, or ordering fields change.

detailSections.title: Main implementations and forms
paragraphs: Do not select a class only because its name is familiar. Select it from the behavior your program needs.

rows: HashMap with elements stored as keys

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: HashSet calls the element's hashCode to locate a HashMap bucket.
It calls equals against candidate keys in that bucket.
If no equal key exists, the element is added as a map key with a shared dummy value.
LinkedHashSet also links entries so iteration follows insertion order.
TreeSet compares from the tree root, moving left or right until it finds comparison zero or an insertion point.
TreeSet's balanced tree keeps height O(log n).
Changing equality/hash/order fields after insertion can make an element visible in iteration but unreachable by contains/remove.
detailSections.note: HashSet is not backed by Hashtable, and TreeSet is not hash-based. HashSet delegates to HashMap; TreeSet delegates to TreeMap.

rows: Boolean result tells whether set changed

Use HashSet when order does not matter.
Use LinkedHashSet when deterministic first-insertion order matters.
Use TreeSet when sorted iteration or range/nearest queries matter.
Use EnumSet for enum flags.

collections.title: Map — key-value storage
collections.summary: A Map stores one value for each unique key and is used when a value must be found from a meaningful identifier.
learningObjectives: Understand keys, values, replacement, and null ambiguity.
Compare HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, and ConcurrentHashMap.
Use compute and merge methods correctly.
Keep map keys stable.
explanation: In one line: A Map stores one value for each unique key and is used when a value must be found from a meaningful identifier.
A Map is like a dictionary: a word is the key and its definition is the value. Keys are unique; values may repeat.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: A Map is like a dictionary: a word is the key and its definition is the value. Keys are unique; values may repeat.
Putting a value for an equal existing key replaces the old value and returns it.
Map does not extend Collection. It exposes collection views through keySet, values, and entrySet.
detailSections.note: Think of employeeId -> Employee. The ID must uniquely and stably identify one employee, while many employees may share the same department value.

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: Hash maps use a key hash to find a candidate bucket, then equals to find the exact key.
TreeMap uses compareTo/Comparator while walking a balanced tree.
put returns the old value when an equal key already exists.
get returns null for both absent and present-with-null in maps that allow null values; containsKey distinguishes them.
entrySet is usually the clearest efficient way to traverse both keys and values.
Default methods such as computeIfAbsent, compute, merge, and replaceAll have exact null/removal rules.
Concurrent atomicity depends on the concrete Map override; HashMap default methods do not make it thread-safe.
detailSections.note: A 'thread-safe map' does not automatically make size-then-put or get-then-put atomic. Prefer one atomic method such as putIfAbsent, compute, or merge on ConcurrentHashMap.

Use LinkedHashMap for deterministic order.
Use TreeMap for sorted key and range operations.

collections.title: HashMap — internal working
collections.summary: HashMap uses a bucket array, hashCode, and equals to provide expected constant-time key lookup.
learningObjectives: Trace put and get internally.
Understand buckets, collisions, load factor, resize, and tree bins.
Apply the equals/hashCode contract.
Know which facts are API contracts and which are Java 17 implementation details.
explanation: In one line: HashMap uses a bucket array, hashCode, and equals to provide expected constant-time key lookup.
HashMap avoids scanning every key. It converts a key's hash into a bucket position and searches only the candidate entries in that bucket.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: HashMap avoids scanning every key. It converts a key's hash into a bucket position and searches only the candidate entries in that bucket.
hashCode does not prove equality. It narrows the search. equals makes the final logical-key decision.
Different keys may share a bucket; this is a collision and is valid. Correctness is preserved by equals, while performance depends on good distribution.
detailSections.note: Imagine a building with numbered rooms. hashCode chooses a room; equals identifies the correct person inside that room. Two people may be assigned the same room without becoming the same person.

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: put receives a key and value.
HashMap obtains the key hashCode and spreads some high bits in the Java 17 implementation.
It calculates a bucket index from the table length.
If the bucket is empty, a new node is placed there.
If entries exist, it compares hash and then equals. An equal key replaces its value; otherwise a collision node is added.
When size crosses capacity multiplied by load factor, the table grows and entries are redistributed.
In Java 17 OpenJDK, a heavily collided eligible bin may change from a linked list to a red-black tree.
get repeats hash/bucket/equality lookup and returns the matching value or null.
detailSections.note: Treeification thresholds and exact resize mechanics describe the Java 17 OpenJDK implementation, not a promise of the Map interface. Mention them as implementation detail, not universal law.

rows: Null may mean absent or mapped-null
Not a concurrency guarantee on HashMap
Function should not structurally modify same map
Lookup fields must still be stable

Iteration order is not part of the result contract.
Keys are immutable or stable for equality/hash purposes.
Access is confined to one thread or safely coordinated externally.
detailSections.note: Avoid or rethink it when: sorted/range access is required, deterministic order matters, or multiple threads mutate it without one synchronization policy.

collections.title: LinkedHashMap — insertion order, access order and LRU
collections.summary: LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that also links entries to provide predictable insertion order or access order.
learningObjectives: Understand its hash table plus linked-order structure.
Distinguish insertion order and access order.
Build a small bounded LRU map correctly.
Understand iterator and concurrency implications.
explanation: In one line: LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that also links entries to provide predictable insertion order or access order.
LinkedHashMap performs key lookup like HashMap and additionally keeps every entry connected in a doubly linked chain.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: LinkedHashMap performs key lookup like HashMap and additionally keeps every entry connected in a doubly linked chain.
By default the chain represents insertion order. Updating an existing value does not create a new insertion position.
With accessOrder=true, successful access operations move an entry toward the most-recent end. The oldest/least-recent entry is at the front.
detailSections.note: The hash table is an index that finds a book quickly; the linked chain is a reading-history list that controls the order in which books are shown.

table.title: LinkedHashMap — insertion order, access order and LRU at a glance
rows: Least recently accessed to most recently accessed.
Replaces value; insertion-order position normally stays.
One null key and multiple null values.
removeEldestEntry after a new mapping is added.

detailSections.title: Main implementations and forms
paragraphs: Do not select a class only because its name is familiar. Select it from the behavior your program needs.

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: A normal hash lookup locates the entry by key.
Each entry also stores before and after links.
Insertion adds a new entry at the tail of the linked order.
In insertion-order mode, reading does not move the entry.
In access-order mode, get and specified update operations relink an accessed entry at the tail.
After a new entry is inserted, removeEldestEntry is called; returning true removes the head.
An access-order get changes structure and can invalidate an active fail-fast iterator.
detailSections.note: An LRU LinkedHashMap is not automatically thread-safe. The cache's get, load, put, eviction, and traversal policy must be coordinated as one design.

rows: May count as access in access mode

You need deterministic deduplication through LinkedHashSet.
A small single-threaded or externally locked LRU policy is sufficient.
HashMap speed is desired with predictable traversal.
detailSections.note: Avoid or rethink it when: you need a scalable concurrent cache, expiration, statistics, refresh, weighted eviction, or persistent ordering.

collections.title: Queue, Deque, PriorityQueue and BlockingQueue
collections.summary: Queue and Deque model processing order; PriorityQueue selects by priority, while BlockingQueue also coordinates producers and consumers.
learningObjectives: Understand FIFO, LIFO, double-ended, and priority processing.
Choose throwing versus special-value method pairs.
Know ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue internals.
Use BlockingQueue instead of manual polling.
explanation: In one line: Queue and Deque model processing order; PriorityQueue selects by priority, while BlockingQueue also coordinates producers and consumers.
Queue commonly processes first-in-first-out: add at the tail and remove from the head.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Queue commonly processes first-in-first-out: add at the tail and remove from the head.
Deque means double-ended queue. It can add/remove at both ends and is Java's preferred general stack through push, pop, and peek.
PriorityQueue does not preserve insertion order. Its head is the least element under natural/default ordering, or the highest priority defined by your Comparator.
BlockingQueue adds waiting operations such as put and take for thread coordination.
detailSections.note: A normal queue is a ticket line, a stack is a pile of plates, a deque has doors at both ends, and a priority queue is an emergency room where priority decides who is next.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: An exception is an object describing a problem that interrupts normal statement-by-statement execution.
When code throws an exception, Java searches for the nearest compatible catch while moving up the call stack. This movement is called stack unwinding.
Exception handling is not only about avoiding a crash. It should protect resources, preserve diagnostic facts, and let the layer that understands the business decision respond.
detailSections.note: Normal flow is a train following its route. Throwing is an emergency signal. Java checks each station/caller for a handler that knows what to do; cleanup still closes doors and protects resources.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: A process is a running program with resources such as memory and files. A thread is one execution path inside that process. Threads share heap objects but have their own call stacks.
Concurrency means tasks make progress during overlapping time. Parallelism means tasks literally execute at the same instant on different CPU cores.
Runnable and Callable describe work. Thread or ExecutorService decides where and when that work runs.

multithreading.title: Java Memory Model and happens-before

explanation: In one line: The Java Memory Model defines when one thread's writes are guaranteed to be visible to another and which program orderings are legal.

Multiple threads may use CPU caches, registers, compiler optimization, and hardware reordering. A write performed by one thread is not automatically guaranteed to be observed by another at the moment you expect.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Multiple threads may use CPU caches, registers, compiler optimization, and hardware reordering. A write performed by one thread is not automatically guaranteed to be observed by another at the moment you expect.
A happens-before relationship is Java's guarantee that actions before one event become visible and ordered before actions after another event.
A data race exists when conflicting accesses to the same variable are not ordered by happens-before and at least one access is a write.
detailSections.note: Each worker may have a local draft. A happens-before rule is the official handover procedure that publishes the finished document before the next worker reads it.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: count++ looks like one line but performs read, calculate, and write. Two threads can read the same old value and one update is lost.

synchronized allows one thread at a time to own the same monitor and also makes prior monitor-protected writes visible to the next owner.

explanation: In one line: Deadlock is permanent waiting caused by a cycle of resource ownership; prevent it with consistent lock order, less locking, or timed/cancellable acquisition.

Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Deadlock occurs when threads are blocked forever because each waits for a resource held by another thread in a cycle.
The classic case is thread A holding lock 1 and waiting for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1.
Deadlock is deterministic in design even if it appears only under rare timing. Fix the locking policy rather than adding sleeps.
detailSections.note: Two cars enter a one-lane crossing from opposite directions. Each owns its current space and waits for the other space; neither can move.

CompletableFuture builds a graph: transform one result, combine independent results, or recover from failure.

explanation: In one line: Java cancellation is cooperative: interruption requests that a task stop, and well-behaved code detects it, cleans up, and propagates or restores the signal.
interrupt does not forcibly kill a thread. It sends a cooperative cancellation signal.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then properties, then internal working, and finally the code example.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: interrupt does not forcibly kill a thread. It sends a cooperative cancellation signal.
Interruptible blocking methods such as sleep, wait, join, take, and many lock operations throw InterruptedException and commonly clear the interrupt status.
If a method cannot propagate InterruptedException, it should usually perform minimal cleanup, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), and return/translate according to its contract.
detailSections.note: Interruption is a fire alarm, not someone physically removing a worker. The worker must notice, leave work in a safe state, and pass the alarm onward if another manager owns the decision.

designPatterns.title: Singleton Design Pattern
designPatterns.summary: The Singleton pattern ensures that a class has one controlled instance and provides a common access point to that instance.

explanation: In one line: Singleton restricts a class to one controlled instance and provides a global access point to it.
The pattern is useful when exactly one shared object should coordinate a resource or service, such as configuration, logging, or a registry.
The important part is not simply making a static object. The class must control construction so callers cannot freely create additional instances.
Study order: first understand the purpose, then the implementation choices, then thread safety, and finally common design problems.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Normally, Java allows a class to be instantiated many times using new. Singleton changes this by making the constructor inaccessible to outside code and exposing one controlled instance.
A typical Singleton has a private constructor, a private static instance field, and a public static method such as getInstance() that returns the instance.
The Singleton instance can be created eagerly when the class is initialized or lazily when it is first requested.
detailSections.note: Think of a building with one security control room. Many employees can access the control room, but the building should not create a separate control room for every employee.

The holder idiom uses Java class initialization guarantees to achieve lazy thread-safe initialization without explicit synchronization.

designPatterns.title: Prototype Design Pattern
designPatterns.summary: The Prototype pattern creates new objects by copying an existing configured object instead of constructing every object from scratch.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and structure of the Prototype pattern.
Distinguish shallow copying from deep copying.
Understand Java clone(), Cloneable, copy constructors, and copy methods.
Recognize when copying an existing object is better than rebuilding it.
Identify common bugs involving shared mutable state.
explanation: In one line: Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing prototype object.
The pattern is useful when object construction is expensive, complicated, or requires many configuration steps.
Instead of repeatedly creating and configuring an object from the beginning, the program keeps a configured prototype and copies it whenever a similar object is required.
Study order: first understand cloning, then shallow versus deep copy, then Java implementation choices, and finally mutable-state bugs.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Suppose an application repeatedly creates reports with the same layout, formatting, and configuration. Instead of rebuilding every report from scratch, it can keep one configured report as a prototype and create copies.
The important question is what gets copied. A shallow copy copies the object's field values, including references. A deep copy also creates independent copies of mutable referenced objects.
Prototype therefore becomes especially important when objects contain nested mutable state.
detailSections.note: Think of a document template. You keep one fully configured template and make a copy whenever a new document is needed.

designPatterns.title: Abstract Factory Design Pattern
designPatterns.summary: The Abstract Factory pattern provides an interface for creating families of related objects without exposing their concrete implementation classes.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and structure of Abstract Factory.
Understand products, concrete products, factories, and concrete factories.
Create related object families without coupling client code to concrete classes.
Understand how Abstract Factory works with interfaces and dependency injection.
Compare Abstract Factory with Factory Method and Builder.
explanation: In one line: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects without requiring client code to know their concrete classes.
The pattern is useful when an application needs multiple related products that must work together, such as a Windows UI family or a Mac UI family.
The client depends on product interfaces and an abstract factory interface. A concrete factory decides which compatible product implementations are created.
Study order: first understand the product family, then the factory structure, then the compatibility benefit, and finally compare it with other creational patterns.

detailSections.title: Simple meaning
paragraphs: Imagine a UI application that supports two themes: Windows and Mac. Each theme requires a compatible Button and Checkbox.
Instead of letting application code directly create WindowsButton, WindowsCheckbox, MacButton, or MacCheckbox, the application asks a factory for a Button and Checkbox.
The selected concrete factory creates the complete compatible family.
detailSections.note: Think of a furniture factory that produces a matching family of Chair, Sofa, and Table. If you choose the modern factory, all products belong to the modern family rather than accidentally mixing incompatible styles.

detailSections.title: Main participants
paragraphs: Abstract Factory becomes easier to understand when the roles are separated.

detailSections.title: How it works internally — step by step
bullets: The application defines interfaces for related product types.
An abstract factory defines creation methods for those product interfaces.
Each concrete factory implements the abstract factory.
A concrete factory creates products from one compatible family.
The client receives the factory and asks it for products.
The client works only with product interfaces.
Changing the product family usually requires changing the factory selection rather than rewriting every product creation call.
Adding a completely new product type requires changes to the abstract factory and all concrete factories.
detailSections.note: Abstract Factory makes it easy to switch product families but makes adding a new product type more expensive because every factory must know how to create that new product.

You expect product families to change independently from client logic.
detailSections.note: Avoid or rethink it when: there is only one unrelated product type or the application does not have a meaningful family of related products. A simpler Factory Method may be enough.

detailSections.title: Small complete example
paragraphs: The client creates a compatible Button and Checkbox through one factory without directly depending on Windows or Mac concrete classes.

detailSections.title: Karat interview answer in 30 seconds

The client depends on the factory and product interfaces, while concrete factories create compatible concrete products. For example, WindowsFactory creates WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox, while MacFactory creates the corresponding Mac products. The major benefit is switching product families without changing client creation logic.
